children.text: Egypt is not a dry country. It is not a country where you can drink the same way everywhere either. What travellers need to understand is less the law than the place, the season, and the social context.
You can drink in Egypt.
This is the answer most travellers want first. In
Cairo
hotel bars, Red Sea resorts, Nile cruise ships, and licensed restaurants, beer, wine, and spirits are served. Local beers such as Stella and Sakara exist, and there is Egyptian-made wine.
That does not make Egyptian alcohol culture simple.

Egypt is a country with a Muslim majority. Many Egyptians do not drink for religious or social reasons. Drunkenness in public is read very negatively. Alcohol exists legally; it is not at the centre of social life.
What travellers need to know is more than whether they can drink.
Where to drink. Where not to expect it. What changes during Ramadan. How to behave in public. Once you have those, you'll get through with no trouble.
Ancient Egypt and alcohol
Egypt's relationship with alcohol is very old.

In ancient Egypt, beer was an everyday drink and a food. It was part of workers' rations and, with bread, supported the basics of life. It was not the cold lager of today — it was thicker, more nutritious, closer to a fermented grain drink.

Wine existed in antiquity too. More expensive than beer, it was tied to royals, temples, and the upper classes. Grape growing and wine production took place in the Nile Delta and along the Mediterranean coast from ancient times.
So Egypt is not historically a country foreign to alcohol.

You cannot simply transplant ancient customs onto the modern society, however. Modern Egypt is a complex layering of Islam, Coptic Christianity, the tourism industry, urban culture, and regional difference.
What you can drink today
The most common local beer is Stella.
It is the lager you'll see in hotels, restaurants, and bars across Egypt, and it suits the heat. Sakara Gold, in a slightly different style, is another local beer.
For wine, there are Egyptian labels — Omar Khayyam, Obelisk, and others. Approach them less as a serious international wine and more as something to try once as a local product.

There is also zibib, an anise-flavoured spirit related to the arak family of the eastern Mediterranean, usually served with water or ice. It is not for every taste, but as a window into the regional drink culture it is interesting.
Imported alcohol is available too, but in hotels and bars it can be expensive. For longer stays or cruises, picking it up at airport duty-free can be more reasonable.
Where you can drink
In Cairo, alcohol is available in international hotels, some restaurants and bars in Zamalek and downtown, and at licensed liquor shops.
Alexandria
also has hotels, some restaurants, and a few bars. As a Mediterranean city, it carries a slightly different atmosphere from Cairo.
In
Luxor
and
Aswan
, hotel bars, Nile cruises, and licensed tourist restaurants serve alcohol. The towns themselves don't move around a drinking culture — these are not places where you go bar-hopping at night.
In the Red Sea resort areas —
Hurghada
, Sharm el-Sheikh,
El Gouna
Marsa Alam
— alcohol is significantly more available. At many resorts and all-inclusive hotels, beer, wine, and cocktails are part of standard service.

In smaller provincial towns, conservative residential areas, and desert oases, alcohol is mostly not available, or you should not expect it at all. In oases such as Siwa, the drinking environment is very limited.
In Egypt, alcohol availability is not uniform across the country. It varies completely by place.
What changes during Ramadan
During Ramadan, alcohol gets harder to find.
There is no nationwide ban, but many restaurants and bars cut back on alcohol service or change their hours. Hotel bars often stay open, sometimes in a more restrained way.
Drinking during the day in front of people who are fasting reads as very inconsiderate. As a traveller, recognise that the social atmosphere changes during Ramadan.
If you travel in this period, plan on drinking only inside hotels or clearly licensed venues. Don't expect ordinary street-level restaurants to serve as usual.
Buying at duty-free
On arrival at Egyptian airports, the duty-free shops can sell imported alcohol.

At international airports in Cairo, Hurghada, Sharm el-Sheikh, Luxor, and Aswan, you may pass through a duty-free shop on arrival. For whisky, gin, vodka, and wine, buying duty-free can be cheaper than ordering glass by glass at hotel bars.
Allowances for import and purchase are subject to change. Confirm the current customs rules before you travel.
If you intend to drink in your own cabin or room on a Nile cruise or a longer resort stay, buying on arrival can be convenient. Not for carrying out to drink in public.
Don't drink in public
The single most important rule in Egypt is: do not drink in public.

On the street, in markets, at sites, in ordinary cafés, in residential areas, or on public transport, do not drink or carry around an open bottle. Before the legal issue, the social objection is strong.
Avoid walking around drunk. Shouting, hassling shopkeepers or passers-by, behaving badly around sites or mosques — these read very poorly in Egypt.
If you drink, drink in places set up for drinking. Hotel bars, licensed restaurants, cruise boats, resort facilities. There, there is no particular problem.
Get the place right. That's the rule.
Women travellers and drinking
Women travellers can drink normally in licensed venues.

How comfortable it feels varies with the place. In international hotel bars, Red Sea resorts, and Nile cruises you will be at ease. In small local-feeling shops or places with only male clientele, drinking alone as a woman stands out.
This is not a legal question. It is the social atmosphere.
For a comfortable drink, choose hotels or restaurants with a good reputation. For late-night moves, use a ride-hailing app or a car arranged through your hotel.
How much to expect
Egypt is not a country you travel to for the alcohol.
There are places where you can have a good beer. A glass while looking at the Nile can become a fond memory. At Red Sea resorts you can drink at the beach or by the pool.
That is not the essence of Egypt.
Alcohol is a supplement to the trip. Temples, tombs, desert, sea, cities, food, encounters with people. Inside that, a drink in the right place. Holding it that way works.
Practical summary
The easiest places to drink are international hotels, licensed restaurants, Nile cruises, and Red Sea resorts.
In small towns, oases, and conservative areas, don't expect it.
During Ramadan, service can be restricted.
Airport duty-free is the practical way to buy imported alcohol — confirm allowances against current rules.
Don't drink in public. Don't walk drunk. Be especially careful near religious sites and ruins.
If you keep to that, you'll rarely have trouble with alcohol in Egypt.
Egypt is a country that has known alcohol since antiquity.
It is also a country where, today, the majority abstain.
Drinking with both of those held in mind is the most important attitude for a traveller.

deck: Can you drink in Egypt? Hotels, restaurants, Red Sea resorts, Ramadan, duty-free, and manners in public — the practical picture travellers need.
